questions.stem: A 69 year old man has 3 months of tiredness and breathlessness walking uphill. He has lost 4 kg without trying. His bowel habit is unchanged and he has seen no blood. He is pale, and there is a firm, non-tender mass in the right iliac fossa.

visual.title: Where the mass is
visual.caption: Right iliac fossa mass: caecal tumour.

questions.q: Where is the lesion most likely to be?
questions.e: Anaemia, weight loss and a right iliac fossa mass with no change in bowel habit is the classic late, silent presentation of a caecal carcinoma.

steps.x: The question asks: Where is the lesion most likely to be? Decide what kind of answer is wanted before reading the options.

clues: firm, non-tender mass in the right iliac fossa
steps.x: Iron-deficiency anaemia plus a RIF mass and no bowel symptoms points to a right-sided tumour.

elim: Left-sided tumours obstruct and change bowel habit early; the mass would be in the left flank.
Rectal cancer gives bleeding, tenesmus and incomplete emptying, and is felt on DRE, not in the RIF.
Sigmoid tumours give rectal bleeding, change in bowel habit and a LIF mass.
A splenic flexure tumour sits in the left upper abdomen and tends to obstruct.

steps.x: A: Caecum. Right-sided = anaemia, weight loss, RIF mass; left-sided = bleeding, change in habit, obstruction.

questions.stem: A 64 year old woman has 3 months of alternating constipation and looser stools, with colicky lower abdominal pain and dark red blood mixed in with the stool. She has lost 3 kg. Her temperature is 36.8°C and pulse rate 84 bpm. There is a vague mass in the left iliac fossa.

visual.title: Where the mass is
visual.caption: Left iliac fossa mass with change in bowel habit.

questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Change in bowel habit, colicky pain, dark blood mixed in, weight loss and a LIF mass is a left-sided (sigmoid) carcinoma; a napkin-ring tumour in the narrow, solid-stool colon obstructs early.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer is wanted before reading the options.

clues: dark red blood mixed in with the stool
mass in the left iliac fossa
steps.x: Months of changed bowel habit with blood and weight loss over 60 is cancer until proven otherwise; LIF means sigmoid.

elim: Diverticulitis is acute, with fever and LIF tenderness, not a 3-month history with weight loss.
Haemorrhoids give bright red blood on the paper, not blood mixed in with a change in bowel habit.
Ischaemic colitis is sudden pain followed by bloody diarrhoea, not months of change in habit.
UC gives bloody diarrhoea with urgency, usually in younger people, not alternating habit and a mass.

steps.x: D: Sigmoid adenocarcinoma. Left-sided tumours present with bleeding, change in bowel habit and obstruction because they encircle a narrow lumen.

questions.stem: A 58 year old man has 2 months of passing blood and mucus, a constant urge to open his bowels and a feeling that he has not emptied them afterwards. He has lost 4 kg. Digital rectal examination shows a hard, irregular, fixed mass 6 cm from the anal verge, with blood on the glove.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Tenesmus, incomplete emptying, bleeding and weight loss with a hard fixed mass on DRE is rectal cancer; over 90% of colorectal cancers are adenocarcinomas.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer is wanted before reading the options.

clues: constant urge to open his bowels
hard, irregular, fixed mass 6 cm from the anal verge
steps.x: Tenesmus plus a hard fixed mass on DRE is rectal cancer; the histological type is almost always adenocarcinoma.

elim: A fissure causes tearing pain on defecation and is seen at the anal margin, not a mass at 6 cm.
Haemorrhoids are soft and usually impalpable on DRE; they do not cause weight loss.
Prolapse is mucosa protruding through the anus, not a hard fixed mass.
Proctitis gives bleeding and urgency but no hard fixed mass or weight loss.

steps.x: C: Rectal adenocarcinoma. Rectal cancer = bleeding, tenesmus, incomplete emptying; always do a DRE.

questions.stem: A 76 year old woman has 3 days of increasing abdominal distension, vomiting and no flatus or stool. She has lost 6 kg over 4 months. She has never had abdominal surgery. Her abdomen is distended and tympanic with high-pitched bowel sounds. Abdominal X-ray shows dilated large bowel up to a cut-off in the sigmoid, with no coffee bean sign.
questions.q: Which is the most likely underlying cause?
questions.e: Colorectal carcinoma is the commonest cause of large bowel obstruction; weight loss before the obstruction supports it. She needs urgent surgical review.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely underlying cause? Decide what kind of answer is wanted before reading the options.
Large bowel obstruction in an older patient with weight loss and no previous surgery is cancer.

elim: Adhesions are the commonest cause of small bowel obstruction and need previous surgery.
Impaction does not cause weight loss and a sharp cut-off; DRE would show hard stool.
A hernia mostly obstructs small bowel and would be found on examining the groins.
Volvulus gives a coffee bean sign on X-ray, which is absent here.

steps.x: B: Colorectal carcinoma. Large bowel obstruction: think cancer first; small bowel obstruction: think adhesions first.

questions.stem: A 24 year old man has a colonoscopy because his father died of bowel cancer aged 39. More than 100 adenomatous polyps carpet the colon. On examination he has a hard bony lump on the mandible, several epidermoid cysts on his back and two extra teeth on dental X-ray.
questions.q: Which gene is most likely to carry the mutation?
questions.e: Hundreds of adenomas with osteomas, epidermoid cysts and supernumerary teeth is Gardner's variant of FAP, caused by a germline APC (tumour suppressor) mutation.

steps.x: The question asks: Which gene is most likely to carry the mutation? Decide what kind of answer is wanted before reading the options.

clues: hard bony lump on the mandible
steps.x: Polyposis plus osteoma, cysts and extra teeth is Gardner's syndrome: APC.

elim: KRAS mutations happen later in the adenoma-carcinoma sequence and are not the inherited defect in polyposis.
MLH1 is a mismatch repair gene mutated in Lynch syndrome, which does not give hundreds of polyps.
STK11 is mutated in Peutz-Jeghers syndrome, with hamartomas and lip pigmentation.
p53 loss is a late step in progression to carcinoma, not the germline cause of polyposis.

steps.x: A: APC. FAP and Gardner's = APC, a tumour suppressor whose loss starts the adenoma-carcinoma sequence.

questions.stem: A 17 year old girl is admitted with colicky abdominal pain. Ultrasound shows a small bowel intussusception. She has dark brown freckles on her lips, inside her mouth and on her palms. Her father has had polyps removed. Capsule endoscopy shows multiple small bowel polyps that are hamartomas on histology.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Hamartomatous GI polyps with pigmented lesions on the lips, mouth and palms, inherited dominantly, is Peutz-Jeghers; polyps can cause intussusception.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer is wanted before reading the options.

clues: dark brown freckles on her lips, inside her mouth and on her palms
steps.x: Pigmented lips plus hamartomatous polyps is Peutz-Jeghers.

elim: FAP gives hundreds of adenomas in the colon, not hamartomas with pigmentation.
Gardner's is FAP with osteomas and cysts, again adenomas not hamartomas.
Lynch causes right-sided cancers with few polyps and no skin pigmentation.
Turcot links colonic polyposis with brain tumours, not mucocutaneous pigmentation.

steps.x: D: Peutz-Jeghers syndrome. Peutz-Jeghers: AD, hamartomas, mucocutaneous pigmentation, raised gastric cancer risk, managed conservatively.

questions.stem: A 35 year old woman has genetic testing after her brother is diagnosed with right-sided colon cancer at 41. She is found to carry a pathogenic MSH2 mutation. She is well and has no symptoms. She asks which other cancer she is at most risk of.
questions.q: Which cancer is she at most increased risk of?
questions.e: MSH2 is a DNA mismatch repair gene: this is Lynch syndrome (HNPCC), which raises the risk of endometrial (the commonest extracolonic cancer), ovarian and sebaceous gland malignancy.

steps.x: The question asks: Which cancer is she at most increased risk of? Decide what kind of answer is wanted before reading the options.
MSH2 = Lynch syndrome; the commonest extracolonic cancer in Lynch is endometrial.

elim: Breast cancer risk is driven by BRCA genes, not mismatch repair genes.
HCC follows cirrhosis and hepatitis B/C, not Lynch syndrome.
Medullary thyroid cancer belongs to MEN2 (RET), not Lynch.
Mesothelioma follows asbestos exposure.

steps.x: B: Endometrial carcinoma. Lynch: right-sided CRC plus endometrial, ovarian and sebaceous tumours.

questions.stem: A 47 year old man has a right hemicolectomy for an ascending colon adenocarcinoma. He also has a sebaceous adenoma on his nose. His father had colon cancer at 52, his paternal aunt had endometrial cancer at 46 and his paternal grandfather had colon cancer at 68. He has no other polyps at colonoscopy.
questions.q: Which is the most likely underlying condition?
questions.e: Three relatives with Lynch-associated cancers, across two generations, one under 50 (3-2-1 rule), plus a right-sided tumour and sebaceous adenoma is Lynch syndrome.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely underlying condition? Decide what kind of answer is wanted before reading the options.
Apply the 3-2-1 rule: 3 relatives, 2 generations, 1 under 50.

elim: FAP gives more than 100 polyps; he has none.
MUTYH polyposis is recessive and gives multiple adenomas, not this dominant cancer pattern.
Peutz-Jeghers gives hamartomas and lip pigmentation.
Three relatives over two generations with one under 50 is not chance.

steps.x: B: Lynch syndrome. Lynch: autosomal dominant, right-sided, few polyps, endometrial/ovarian/sebaceous tumours.

questions.stem: A 68 year old woman has a sigmoid colectomy after a screening FIT led to colonoscopy. Histology shows an adenocarcinoma confined to the submucosa, not reaching the muscularis propria. None of 16 lymph nodes contain tumour. CT chest, abdomen and pelvis shows no metastases.
questions.q: Which is the Duke's stage?
questions.e: Tumour confined beneath the muscularis propria with no nodal or distant spread is Duke's A.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the Duke's stage? Decide what kind of answer is wanted before reading the options.

clues: confined to the submucosa, not reaching the muscularis propria
steps.x: Ask in order: through the muscle? nodes? distant spread? Here no to all.

elim: Stage B needs invasion into the muscularis propria, which has not happened.
C1 needs regional lymph node involvement.
C2 needs the apical node to be involved.
Stage D needs distant metastases.

steps.x: A: A. Duke's: A = beneath muscularis propria; B = into it; C = nodes; D = distant metastases.

questions.stem: A 71 year old man has a left hemicolectomy for a descending colon adenocarcinoma. Histology shows tumour invading through the muscularis propria. Five of 18 lymph nodes contain tumour, including the apical node at the highest point of the vascular tie. CT shows no liver or lung lesions.
questions.q: Which is the Duke's stage?
questions.e: Muscle invasion with regional nodes and an involved apical node, but no distant spread, is Duke's C2.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the Duke's stage? Decide what kind of answer is wanted before reading the options.

clues: Five of 18 lymph nodes contain tumour
steps.x: Nodes positive = C; apical node involved = C2 rather than C1.

elim: Stage A tumours are confined beneath the muscularis propria.
Stage B has no nodal involvement.
C1 is nodal spread with the apical node spared.
There are no distant metastases on CT.

steps.x: D: C2. C1: apical node clear (about 40% 5-year survival); C2: apical node involved.

questions.stem: A 73 year old woman has a caecal adenocarcinoma on colonoscopy. Staging CT shows tumour through the bowel wall, enlarged regional nodes and three low-attenuation lesions in the liver. She feels well apart from tiredness.
questions.q: Which is the Duke's stage?
questions.e: Any distant metastasis, here in the liver, makes it Duke's D. Colorectal cancer spreads to the liver first because the colon drains via the portal vein.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the Duke's stage? Decide what kind of answer is wanted before reading the options.

clues: three low-attenuation lesions in the liver
steps.x: Distant spread trumps everything else in staging.

elim: The tumour has spread far beyond the mucosa and submucosa.
B has no nodal or distant spread.
Liver metastases outrank nodal disease.
C stages have no distant metastases.

steps.x: E: D. Duke's D = distant metastases; the liver is the commonest site (portal venous drainage); check LFTs.

questions.stem: A 72 year old man has 2 months of rectal bleeding and tenesmus. Biopsy confirms a rectal adenocarcinoma. He had external beam radiotherapy for prostate cancer 11 years ago. He has hypertension and had an appendicectomy aged 20. He eats a vegetarian, high-fibre diet and has never smoked.
questions.q: Which is the most important risk factor for his cancer?
questions.e: External beam radiotherapy for prostate cancer raises the later risk of rectal cancer. Other risks are age, smoking, obesity and a low-fibre diet.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most important risk factor for his cancer? Decide what kind of answer is wanted before reading the options.

clues: external beam radiotherapy for prostate cancer 11 years ago
steps.x: The rectum lies in the prostate radiotherapy field; this is a named risk factor in the notes.

elim: Previous appendicectomy is not a risk factor for colorectal cancer.
A high-fibre diet is protective; low fibre is the risk factor.
Hypertension is not a recognised risk factor.
Red and processed meat raise risk; a vegetarian diet does not.

steps.x: D: Previous pelvic radiotherapy. Risk factors: age, polyps, Lynch, FAP, IBD, previous pelvic radiotherapy, smoking, obesity, low fibre.

questions.stem: A 74 year old man with a known sigmoid tumour awaiting surgery develops sudden severe generalised abdominal pain. His temperature is 38.1°C, pulse rate 118 bpm, BP 96/60 mmHg and respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute. His abdomen is rigid with guarding everywhere. Erect chest X-ray (see item resources) is shown.

visual.title: Erect chest X-ray
visual.caption: Free air under both hemidiaphragms: perforated viscus.

questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Peritonitis with free air under the diaphragm in a patient with a known colorectal tumour is a perforation, a recognised complication of the tumour itself.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer is wanted before reading the options.
Rigid abdomen plus free subdiaphragmatic gas means perforation; the tumour is the cause.

elim: Ischaemia gives pain out of proportion to signs and no free air.
He has not had an operation yet, so there is no anastomosis.
Obstruction gives distension and vomiting, not a rigid abdomen with free air.
Possible in theory, but with a known sigmoid tumour the perforation is colonic.

steps.x: C: Colonic perforation. Tumour complications: obstruction, perforation, bleeding/anaemia, liver metastases, cachexia.

questions.stem: A 61 year old woman has a colonoscopy after a positive screening FIT. A 2.5 cm tubulovillous adenoma with low-grade dysplasia is found in the sigmoid colon. There is no invasion on histology. She asks what this lesion means.
questions.q: Which best describes this lesion?
o: Benign polyp with no malignant potential
questions.e: Adenomas are pre-malignant and progress to carcinoma over years via the adenoma-to-carcinoma sequence, which is why they are removed.

steps.x: The question asks: Which best describes this lesion? Decide what kind of answer is wanted before reading the options.
Adenoma with dysplasia but no invasion = pre-malignant; large and villous adenomas carry most risk.

elim: Adenomas do have malignant potential; hyperplastic polyps are the ones that rarely do.
Hamartomas are the polyps of Peutz-Jeghers, not tubulovillous adenomas.
Pseudopolyps form in IBD and are not dysplastic.
There is no invasion on histology.

steps.x: E: Pre-malignant polyp. Most colorectal cancers arise from adenomatous polyps via the adenoma-to-carcinoma sequence.

questions.stem: A 66 year old man is 6 days after a right hemicolectomy with primary anastomosis. He has type 2 diabetes and smokes. He has become confused, has not passed flatus and has worsening abdominal pain. His temperature is 38.6°C, pulse rate 112 bpm, BP 104/66 mmHg and respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute. His abdomen is tender around the wound.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Abdominal pain, fever, delirium, prolonged ileus and sepsis at 5 to 7 days after a bowel anastomosis is an anastomotic leak; diabetes and smoking raise the risk.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer is wanted before reading the options.
Day 5 to 7 sepsis after an anastomosis is a leak until proven otherwise.

elim: Pneumonia gives cough and chest signs, not worsening abdominal pain and ileus.
PE gives breathlessness and pleuritic pain, not fever with abdominal tenderness.
Wound infection gives local erythema and pus, not ileus and sepsis.
UTI does not explain prolonged ileus and abdominal pain.

steps.x: A: Anastomotic leak. Leak risk factors: smoking, diabetes, immunosuppression, alcohol, obesity, malnutrition, emergency surgery, long operation.

questions.stem: A 67 year old man had a FIT test for 2 months of looser stools. His FIT result is 85 micrograms of haemoglobin per gram of faeces. He is referred on the suspected cancer pathway. He is fit and well otherwise.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?
questions.e: Colonoscopy with biopsy is the gold standard: it sees the whole colon, confirms histology and can remove polyps.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation? Decide what kind of answer is wanted before reading the options.
FIT above 10 means urgent colonoscopy; tissue confirms the diagnosis.

elim: Barium enema is outdated and cannot take a biopsy.
CT colonography is for when colonoscopy fails or is not tolerated; it cannot biopsy.
Sigmoidoscopy only sees the left colon and could miss a right-sided tumour.
CEA monitors treatment response; it is not diagnostic.

steps.x: B: Colonoscopy and biopsy. Gold standard for colorectal cancer: colonoscopy plus biopsy.

questions.stem: A 52 year old woman sees her GP with 6 weeks of unexplained weight loss of 5 kg and vague abdominal pain. Her bowel habit is normal. Examination is unremarkable. A FIT test is sent and returns 24 micrograms of haemoglobin per gram of faeces.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step?
o: Reassure and repeat FIT in 6 months
questions.e: Age 40 or over with unexplained weight loss and abdominal pain is a FIT indication; a result of 10 micrograms or more means 2-week-wait referral for urgent colonoscopy.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the next most appropriate step? Decide what kind of answer is wanted before reading the options.
Threshold is 10: she is above it.

elim: Ultrasound does not assess the colon mucosa.
A FIT of 10 or more is positive and must not be watched.
A positive FIT needs the urgent 2-week-wait pathway, not routine.
CEA is not a diagnostic or triage test.

steps.x: E: Suspected cancer referral for colonoscopy. FIT is first-line in primary care; 10 micrograms or above = 2-week-wait colonoscopy (NICE).

questions.stem: A 63 year old woman has a routine blood test before a knee replacement. She has no bowel symptoms and no rectal bleeding. Examination including abdomen is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step?
o: Reassure and repeat FBC in 3 months
questions.e: NICE: unexplained anaemia at 60 or over, even without iron deficiency, should prompt a FIT and assessment for colorectal cancer.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate next step? Decide what kind of answer is wanted before reading the options.
Over 60 with anaemia = colorectal cancer triage, even if ferritin is normal.

elim: There is no pancytopenia or blood film abnormality to justify marrow examination.
This is a second-line test when colonoscopy fails, not the triage step.
Unexplained anaemia over 60 is a referral trigger and must be investigated.
CEA is for monitoring, not detecting cancer.

steps.x: C: Faecal immunochemical test. FIT first-line triage; anaemia at 60 or over (with or without iron deficiency) triggers it.

questions.stem: A 79 year old woman with change in bowel habit and a FIT of 60 micrograms has a colonoscopy. The scope cannot pass beyond the sigmoid because of severe looping and diverticular disease. She is keen to avoid another attempt. She is otherwise well.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
questions.e: CT colonography is the second-line test when colonoscopy fails; it images the whole colon and can also detect liver metastases.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate next investigation? Decide what kind of answer is wanted before reading the options.
Failed colonoscopy = CT colonography.

elim: A plain film cannot show a mucosal tumour.
A barium meal looks at the stomach, not the colon.
Capsule endoscopy is for the small bowel and cannot be used safely to clear the colon here.
MRI pelvis stages rectal cancer; it does not image the whole colon.

steps.x: D: CT colonography. CT colonography: when colonoscopy fails or is not tolerated; also shows extracolonic disease.

questions.stem: A 61 year old man has a biopsy-proven adenocarcinoma of the mid rectum. CT chest, abdomen and pelvis shows no distant metastases. The multidisciplinary team needs to know the depth of invasion and the relation of the tumour to the mesorectal fascia before planning treatment.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
questions.e: MRI pelvis locally stages rectal cancer (depth, nodes, circumferential margin) and decides whether neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy is needed; CT CAP covers distant spread.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate investigation? Decide what kind of answer is wanted before reading the options.
Local rectal staging = MRI pelvis; distant staging = CT chest, abdomen and pelvis.

elim: CT colonography finds colonic lesions but does not define the mesorectal margin well.
The tumour is already found and biopsied.
PET-CT is for problem-solving distant disease, not local rectal staging.
CEA gives no anatomical information.

steps.x: C: MRI pelvis. Rectal cancer: MRI pelvis for local staging before surgery ± neoadjuvant treatment.

questions.stem: A 66 year old woman had a left hemicolectomy for Duke's C1 descending colon cancer 2 years ago. She is well. At follow-up her carcinoembryonic antigen has risen from 2.1 to 14 micrograms/L over 6 months. Her LFTs show ALP 210 U/L (30–130).

visual.title: CEA after surgery
visual.caption: A steadily rising CEA suggests recurrence.

questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
questions.e: CEA is used to monitor treatment response and detect recurrence; a rising CEA with raised ALP suggests liver metastases and needs CT chest, abdomen and pelvis.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate next investigation? Decide what kind of answer is wanted before reading the options.
Rising CEA after resection = look for recurrence with CT.

elim: A plain film cannot show liver or lung metastases.
FIT is a primary care triage test, not for follow-up of known cancer.
A rising CEA needs imaging now, not a wait.
Another marker adds nothing; the recurrence must be located.

steps.x: B: CT chest, abdomen and pelvis. CEA is a monitoring marker, not a diagnostic test; CT CAP stages and restages.

questions.stem: A 52 year old man asks his GP about the NHS bowel cancer screening programme. He has no bowel symptoms and no family history of bowel cancer. His examination is normal.
questions.q: Which screening test is offered to him?
o: Annual guaiac faecal occult blood test
questions.e: The NHS bowel cancer screening programme sends a home FIT kit every 2 years to people aged 50 to 74; a positive result leads to colonoscopy.

steps.x: The question asks: Which screening test is offered to him? Decide what kind of answer is wanted before reading the options.
Average-risk screening is FIT, every 2 years, ages 50 to 74.

elim: Guaiac FOB has been replaced by FIT in England.
CEA is not a screening test.
Screening colonoscopy is only for positive FIT or high-risk groups.
Routine screening uses FIT, not repeated sigmoidoscopy.

steps.x: D: FIT every 2 years from 50 to 74. Bowel cancer screening programme: FIT every 2 years, 50 to 74.

questions.stem: A 71 year old woman is 6 days after an anterior resection for rectal cancer. She has a temperature of 38.0°C, pulse rate 104 bpm and BP 128/78 mmHg. She has lower abdominal discomfort and has not passed flatus for 2 days, but her abdomen is soft without peritonism. She is otherwise stable.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to confirm the suspected complication?
questions.e: Suspected anastomotic leak in a stable patient is shown with a water-soluble (Gastrografin) contrast enema; CT abdomen and pelvis comes first if peritonitic or shocked.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate investigation to confirm the suspected complication? Decide what kind of answer is wanted before reading the options.

clues: has not passed flatus for 2 days
steps.x: Fever and ileus at day 6 after a low anastomosis is a leak; stable, so contrast enema.

elim: Ultrasound cannot show contrast escaping from the anastomosis.
A plain film shows ileus but cannot show a leak.
Barium leaking into the peritoneum causes severe peritonitis; use water-soluble contrast.
Insufflating a fresh anastomosis risks making a leak worse.

steps.x: E: Gastrografin enema. Leak: Gastrografin enema (CT first if peritonitic shock); treat with IV antibiotics and laparotomy.

questions.stem: A 58 year old man has a screening colonoscopy after a positive FIT. A single 12 mm pedunculated polyp is found in the sigmoid colon. The rest of the colon is normal. He has no symptoms.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management of the polyp?
o: Leave it and repeat colonoscopy in 5 years
questions.e: Benign or pre-malignant polyps are removed endoscopically (polypectomy), which interrupts the adenoma-to-carcinoma sequence and gives histology.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate management of the polyp? Decide what kind of answer is wanted before reading the options.
A pedunculated polyp is removed at colonoscopy.

elim: Hartmann's is an emergency operation for perforation or obstruction.
Adenomas progress to cancer, so it should be removed now.
There is no cancer to treat.
Resection is not needed for a polyp that can be removed endoscopically.

steps.x: A: Endoscopic polypectomy. First-line treatment for polyps: polypectomy at colonoscopy.

questions.stem: A 64 year old woman has a biopsy-proven adenocarcinoma of the descending colon, 8 cm below the splenic flexure. Staging CT shows no metastases. She is fit for surgery and the multidisciplinary team recommends curative resection.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate operation?
questions.e: Distal transverse and descending colon tumours, up to the splenic flexure, are treated with a left hemicolectomy.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate operation? Decide what kind of answer is wanted before reading the options.
Match the operation to the territory: descending colon = left hemicolectomy.

elim: AP resection is for low rectal tumours.
Anterior resection is for rectal tumours.
Hartmann's is an emergency operation, not elective curative surgery.
Right hemicolectomy is for caecal, ascending and proximal transverse tumours.

steps.x: D: Left hemicolectomy. Right: caecum to proximal transverse; left: distal transverse to descending; sigmoid: high anterior resection.

questions.stem: A 70 year old man has an elective work-up for a sigmoid colon adenocarcinoma found at colonoscopy. CT chest, abdomen and pelvis shows no distant spread. He is not obstructed and is fit for a curative operation.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate operation?
questions.e: An elective sigmoid cancer is treated with a sigmoid colectomy (high anterior resection) with primary anastomosis.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate operation? Decide what kind of answer is wanted before reading the options.
Elective sigmoid tumour = high anterior resection; emergency sigmoid tumour = Hartmann's.

elim: AP resection removes the anus for low rectal tumours.
Hartmann's is used in the emergency setting of obstruction or perforation.
Left hemicolectomy covers the descending colon, not a sigmoid tumour.
Removing the whole colon and rectum is for FAP, not a single sporadic tumour.

steps.x: C: High anterior resection. Sigmoid cancer: sigmoid colectomy (high anterior resection).

questions.stem: A 59 year old woman has an adenocarcinoma of the upper rectum, 12 cm from the anal verge. MRI pelvis shows a clear circumferential margin and CT shows no metastases. The multidisciplinary team recommends surgery.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate operation?
questions.e: Rectal tumours more than 8 cm from the anal verge (proximal third) are treated with an anterior resection and a temporary defunctioning loop ileostomy, the commonest rectal cancer operation.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate operation? Decide what kind of answer is wanted before reading the options.
More than 8 cm from the verge = sphincter can be saved = anterior resection.

elim: AP resection is for tumours within 8 cm of the anal verge.
Hartmann's is for emergencies.
This does not remove a rectal tumour.
This is for right-sided colon tumours.

steps.x: B: Anterior resection with loop ileostomy. Rectal cancer: within 8 cm = AP resection; above 8 cm = anterior resection with temporary loop ileostomy.

questions.stem: A 75 year old man has iron-deficiency anaemia. Colonoscopy and biopsy show an adenocarcinoma at the hepatic flexure. Staging CT shows no metastases. He is fit for surgery.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate operation?
questions.e: Caecal, ascending and proximal transverse colon (hepatic flexure) tumours are treated by right hemicolectomy, usually with a primary ileocolic anastomosis.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate operation? Decide what kind of answer is wanted before reading the options.
Hepatic flexure is on the right side of the colon.

elim: Anterior resection is for rectal tumours.
Hartmann's is for emergency sigmoid disease.
Left hemicolectomy is for the distal transverse and descending colon.
This is for FAP, not a single sporadic tumour.

steps.x: D: Right hemicolectomy. Right hemicolectomy for caecum, ascending colon and proximal transverse colon; extended for transverse tumours.

questions.stem: A 21 year old woman has known familial adenomatous polyposis. Her latest colonoscopy shows several hundred adenomas throughout the colon and rectum, some with high-grade dysplasia. She wants to discuss definitive treatment.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
questions.e: FAP carries almost certain colorectal cancer, so the whole colon and rectum are removed (total proctocolectomy) with an ileal pouch-anal anastomosis.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate management? Decide what kind of answer is wanted before reading the options.
All the mucosa is at risk, so all of it comes out.

elim: Hundreds of polyps cannot all be removed, and cancer is inevitable.
This leaves most of the at-risk colon and the rectum.
Chemoprevention does not remove the near-certain cancer risk.
This leaves the left colon and rectum at risk.

steps.x: E: Total proctocolectomy with ileal pouch. FAP: total proctocolectomy with ileal pouch.

questions.stem: A 77 year old woman has a perforated sigmoid carcinoma with faecal peritonitis. She has been resuscitated with IV fluids and antibiotics and goes to theatre. Her pulse rate is 120 bpm and BP 90/58 mmHg despite fluids. The surgeon finds gross faecal contamination.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate operation?
questions.e: Hartmann's procedure (sigmoid colectomy with end colostomy and closed rectal stump) is used for a perforated or obstructing sigmoid tumour; an end colostomy is safer than an anastomosis in an emergency.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate operation? Decide what kind of answer is wanted before reading the options.
Emergency, contaminated, unstable = no anastomosis = end colostomy.

elim: A stent treats obstruction, not perforation with peritonitis.
Lavage leaves the perforated tumour in place.
The tumour is in the sigmoid.
An anastomosis in a shocked, contaminated abdomen has a high leak risk.

steps.x: B: Hartmann's procedure. Hartmann's: sigmoid resection plus end colostomy for perforation or malignant obstruction.

questions.stem: An 82 year old man has a descending colon cancer with widespread liver and lung metastases. He has 4 days of distension and absolute constipation that has not settled with nasogastric decompression and IV fluids. CT confirms obstruction at the tumour. He wants to avoid a stoma.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
questions.e: A palliative self-expanding stent relieves obstruction in stage IV disease that has not settled with conservative treatment, and avoids a stoma.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate management? Decide what kind of answer is wanted before reading the options.
Stage IV plus refractory obstruction = stent.

elim: This is a curative operation for low rectal cancer, not for stage IV colonic disease.
Conservative treatment has already failed; he risks perforation.
Major resection is not appropriate with widespread metastases.
This is far too extensive and is for FAP.

steps.x: D: Palliative colonic stent. Advanced disease: oncology, palliative chemotherapy, stenting or symptom control.

questions.stem: A 63 year old man is having an elective left hemicolectomy for colon cancer on an enhanced recovery pathway. The anaesthetist discusses post-operative pain relief. He has no contraindications to any technique.
questions.q: Which analgesic approach best speeds the return of bowel function?
questions.e: Epidural analgesia reduces systemic opioid use and sympathetic inhibition of the gut, accelerating the return of bowel function after colorectal surgery.

steps.x: The question asks: Which analgesic approach best speeds the return of bowel function? Decide what kind of answer is wanted before reading the options.
Opioids cause ileus; the epidural avoids most of them.

elim: Opioids slow gut motility and delay recovery of bowel function.
Systemic opioids prolong post-operative ileus.
Uncontrolled pain is unsafe and also slows recovery.
Codeine is an opioid and is constipating.

steps.x: E: Thoracic epidural analgesia. Epidural analgesia accelerates return of bowel function after colorectal surgery.

questions.stem: A 68 year old woman has a sigmoid adenocarcinoma. Staging CT shows multiple bilateral liver metastases and lung nodules that the multidisciplinary team judges unresectable. She is not obstructed, has mild anaemia, and remains active with a performance status of 1.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
questions.e: Unresectable metastatic (Duke's D) disease in a fit patient is treated with oncology input and palliative chemotherapy; stents and symptom control are kept for complications.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate management? Decide what kind of answer is wanted before reading the options.
Stage IV, fit and not obstructed = systemic treatment.

elim: AP resection is for low rectal cancer and would not cure stage IV disease.
A stent is for obstruction, which she does not have.
There is no emergency such as perforation or obstruction.
Doing nothing active wastes the benefit of chemotherapy in a fit patient.

steps.x: D: Palliative chemotherapy under oncology. Metastatic disease: oncology, palliative chemotherapy, stenting or symptom control.

questions.stem: A 66 year old man has a rectal adenocarcinoma 3 cm from the anal verge that involves the anal sphincter on MRI. He has completed neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy and is listed for an abdomino-perineal resection. He asks what he will have afterwards.
questions.q: Which will he most likely be left with?
questions.e: AP resection removes the rectum, anal canal and anus (with sphincter for low tumours), leaving a permanent end colostomy.

steps.x: The question asks: Which will he most likely be left with? Decide what kind of answer is wanted before reading the options.
No anus left = permanent end colostomy.

elim: The anus and sphincter are removed, so there is nowhere for stool to pass.
The colon is kept, so the stoma is a colostomy, not an ileostomy.
There is no distal bowel to rejoin, so it cannot be reversed.
A temporary loop ileostomy goes with an anterior resection.

steps.x: B: Permanent end colostomy. AP resection: tumours within 8 cm of the verge; permanent end colostomy.

questions.stem: A 57 year old woman has a mid-rectal adenocarcinoma. MRI pelvis shows tumour extending to within 1 mm of the mesorectal fascia with several enlarged mesorectal nodes. CT chest, abdomen and pelvis shows no distant metastases.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
questions.e: Rectal cancer is treated with surgery with or without neoadjuvant radiotherapy or chemoradiotherapy; a threatened margin and nodes on MRI mean shrinking the tumour first.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the next most appropriate step in management? Decide what kind of answer is wanted before reading the options.

clues: within 1 mm of the mesorectal fascia
steps.x: MRI decides: a threatened margin means downstage first, then operate.

elim: This is an emergency operation, not planned rectal cancer surgery.
With a threatened margin, surgery first risks leaving tumour behind.
There are no metastases; this is potentially curable.
This is an invasive cancer, not a polyp.

steps.x: C: Neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy. Rectal cancer: MRI pelvis, then surgery ± neoadjuvant (chemo)radiotherapy.

questions.stem: A 39 year old man has a right-sided colon adenocarcinoma. His mother had endometrial cancer at 44. Immunohistochemistry shows loss of MLH1 protein in the tumour. Colonoscopy found no other polyps.
questions.q: Which molecular finding is most likely in the tumour?
questions.e: Lynch syndrome is caused by germline mutations in DNA mismatch repair genes (MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2); failed repair causes microsatellite instability and a fast route to right-sided cancer, often without an obvious adenoma.

steps.x: The question asks: Which molecular finding is most likely in the tumour? Decide what kind of answer is wanted before reading the options.
MLH1 is a mismatch repair gene; mismatch repair failure leaves microsatellites unstable.

elim: This is the Philadelphia chromosome of chronic myeloid leukaemia.
HER2 amplification is a feature of some breast and gastric cancers.
STK11 loss causes Peutz-Jeghers syndrome.
Repeat expansions cause disorders such as Huntington's, not cancer.

steps.x: D: Microsatellite instability. Lynch: mismatch repair defect, microsatellite instability, accelerated right-sided CRC.

questions.stem: A 70 year old man has a sigmoid colectomy. Histology shows an invasive adenocarcinoma arising within a residual tubulovillous adenoma. A pathologist explains that the tumour developed through a series of mutations over many years.
questions.q: Which mutation is most associated with the final step from adenoma to invasive carcinoma?
questions.e: In the adenoma-to-carcinoma sequence, APC loss starts the adenoma, KRAS activation grows it, and p53 loss late on drives invasion.

steps.x: The question asks: Which mutation is most associated with the final step from adenoma to invasive carcinoma? Decide what kind of answer is wanted before reading the options.

clues: invasive adenocarcinoma arising within a residual tubulovillous adenoma
series of mutations over many years
steps.x: Order: APC (start), KRAS (growth), p53 (invasion).

elim: APC loss is the early, initiating step that starts adenoma formation.
BRCA1 is linked to breast and ovarian cancer.
KRAS activation drives adenoma growth in the middle of the sequence.
RET mutations cause MEN2 and medullary thyroid cancer.

steps.x: E: TP53 loss. Most CRC arises by the adenoma-to-carcinoma sequence: APC, KRAS, p53.

questions.stem: A 78 year old woman has a 7 cm caecal adenocarcinoma found during investigation of iron-deficiency anaemia. She has never had abdominal distension, vomiting or change in bowel habit. Her daughter asks why such a large tumour caused no blockage.
questions.q: Which best explains the lack of obstruction?
o: Peristalsis is absent in the caecum
Wide lumen and liquid stool in the caecum
questions.e: Right-sided tumours grow exophytically into a wide-calibre caecum full of semi-liquid stool, so they bleed occultly and cause anaemia rather than obstruction, presenting late.

steps.x: The question asks: Which best explains the lack of obstruction? Decide what kind of answer is wanted before reading the options.
Think about the lumen: wide and liquid on the right, narrow and solid on the left.

elim: This is an adenocarcinoma; site does not decide malignancy.
Circumferential napkin-ring growth is typical of left-sided tumours and does obstruct.
The caecum does contract; this is not the reason.
Metastasis does not prevent local growth.

steps.x: E: Wide lumen and liquid stool in the caecum. Right = wide, liquid, occult bleeding, late; left = narrow, solid, obstruction, early.

questions.stem: A 65 year old man has a sigmoid adenocarcinoma. CT shows an apple-core stricture in the sigmoid colon and several metastases in the liver but none in the lungs. He asks why the cancer has gone to his liver first.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation?
o: Lymphatic drainage to the thoracic duct
Transcoelomic spread to the liver capsule
Venous drainage via the portal vein
questions.e: Blood from the colon drains through the mesenteric veins into the portal vein, so the liver is the first capillary bed that tumour cells meet. The apple-core lesion reflects circumferential napkin-ring growth.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely explanation? Decide what kind of answer is wanted before reading the options.

clues: metastases in the liver but none in the lungs
steps.x: Follow the blood: colon to portal vein to liver.

elim: The sigmoid is far from the liver; spread is not by direct invasion.
Lymphatic spread goes to regional nodes and would reach the lungs before the liver.
Ureters do not carry tumour to the liver.
Peritoneal seeding gives deposits on surfaces, not intrahepatic metastases.

steps.x: E: Venous drainage via the portal vein. Tumour complications: obstruction, liver metastases (portal drainage), perforation, anaemia, cachexia.

questions.stem: A 72 year old woman with a known ascending colon carcinoma has lost 9 kg over 3 months. She has muscle wasting and temporal hollowing despite eating reasonably. Her albumin is 28 g/L (35–50) and haemoglobin 92 g/L (115–165). She has no obstruction.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of her weight loss?
questions.e: Cachexia, wasting driven by tumour-related inflammatory cytokines despite reasonable intake, is a complication of the tumour itself, alongside anaemia and perforation.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely cause of her weight loss? Decide what kind of answer is wanted before reading the options.
Wasting despite eating in known cancer = cachexia.

elim: There is no restriction of intake or body image disturbance.
Coeliac disease does not explain this in a patient with a known carcinoma.
There are no thyroid features such as tremor or tachycardia.
She has no obstructive symptoms.

steps.x: B: Cancer cachexia. Tumour complications: obstruction, liver metastases, perforation, anaemia, cachexia.
